accepted.label: Naive Bayes Classifier Core
accepted.description: Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier that applies Bayes' theorem with the naive assumption of feature independence given the class. It computes posterior probability for each class and predicts the one with maximum probability.
coverage_criteria: State the naive independence assumption.
Describe how Naive Bayes uses Bayes theorem for classification.
Identify that it is an eager learning algorithm.
accepted.merge_rationale: These three candidates all describe the core Naive Bayes algorithm from different sources, covering the probabilistic basis, the naive assumption, and its application to text classification.

accepted.label: Probability Foundations for Naive Bayes
accepted.description: Foundational probability concepts: basic probability, conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), and Bayes theorem P(B|A) = P(A|B)P(B)/P(A) with posterior, likelihood, prior, and evidence.
coverage_criteria: State the formula for conditional probability.
Write Bayes theorem and name the terms.
Compute a simple probability using the formula.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates build the mathematical prerequisites for Naive Bayes: probability, conditional probability, and Bayes theorem, which are often taught together.

accepted.label: Feature Independence Assumption and Multicollinearity
accepted.description: Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class (the 'naive' assumption). Multicollinearity (high feature correlation) violates this independence, causing poor performance.
coverage_criteria: Explain the naive independence assumption.
Define multicollinearity and its impact on Naive Bayes.
Describe a method to detect multicollinearity.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates explain the independence assumption and the related issue of multicollinearity, forming a single concept about why the algorithm is called naive and a key limitation.

accepted.label: Naive Bayes Variants: Bernoulli, Multinomial, Gaussian
accepted.description: Three main variants: Bernoulli for binary features, Multinomial for discrete counts (especially text), and Gaussian for continuous features assuming a normal distribution.
coverage_criteria: Match each variant to its typical data type.
Identify the appropriate variant for a given scenario.
Recognize scikit-learn class names for each variant.
accepted.merge_rationale: These three candidates describe the distinct variants of Naive Bayes, each tailored to different feature types, and are best taught as a comparative set.

accepted.label: Zero Frequency Error and Laplace Smoothing
accepted.description: Zero frequency error occurs when a test feature value was not seen during training, causing zero posterior probability. Laplace smoothing adds a small constant (usually 1) to counts to avoid zeros.
coverage_criteria: Define zero frequency error.
Explain how Laplace smoothing mitigates the error.
Describe the effect of the smoothing parameter α.
accepted.merge_rationale: The zero frequency error and its standard solution (Laplace smoothing) are closely linked and form a natural teachable unit.

accepted.label: Practical Aspects of Naive Bayes: Applications, Advantages, and Usage
accepted.description: Naive Bayes is used in text classification, sentiment analysis, recommendation, and real-time prediction. Advantages: fast, less training data (when independent), good with categorical/text data. Disadvantages: independence assumption, zero frequency. Best when features are fairly independent and for text tasks.
coverage_criteria: List at least three real-world applications.
State two advantages and two disadvantages.
Describe scenarios where Naive Bayes is a good choice or should be avoided.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates collectively cover when and why to use Naive Bayes, combining applications, pros/cons, and usage guidelines into one practical concept.

accepted.label: Improving Naive Bayes Performance
accepted.description: Techniques include removing correlated features, feature engineering, domain knowledge, using probabilistic features, Laplace smoothing, and the log-trick for numerical stability: argmax (log prior + Σ log P(xᵢ|y)).
coverage_criteria: Name at least three improvement strategies.
Explain why the log-trick is used.
Apply the log-trick in a posterior calculation.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates address enhancing Naive Bayes; the log-trick is a specific, important technique within the broader set of improvement strategies.

accepted.label: Gaussian Naive Bayes: Prior, Likelihood, and PDF
accepted.description: In Gaussian Naive Bayes, the prior P(y) is the class frequency. The class conditional probability P(xᵢ|y) is modeled with a Gaussian PDF: (1/√(2πσ²)) exp(-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)), where μ and σ² are estimated per feature per class.
coverage_criteria: Calculate prior probabilities from a dataset.
Write the Gaussian PDF formula.
Compute a PDF value given mean and variance.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates detail the Gaussian-specific components: prior estimation, the rationale for the Gaussian assumption, and the exact formula, which together form the mathematical core of Gaussian Naive Bayes.

accepted.label: Naive Bayes Training and Prediction Procedure
accepted.description: Training: compute per-class means, variances, and prior probabilities. Prediction: choose the class with the highest log-posterior: log P(y) + Σ log P(xᵢ|y) using argmax.
coverage_criteria: List the statistics computed during training.
Explain the prediction step using argmax.
Perform a simple prediction by hand for a small dataset.
accepted.merge_rationale: Training and prediction are the two essential phases of the Naive Bayes workflow, logically linked as a single concept.

accepted.label: Implementing Naive Bayes in Python
accepted.description: The classifier is implemented as a Python class with fit() and predict() methods, using NumPy arrays, storing learned parameters as attributes. Model performance is evaluated using accuracy on a test set.
coverage_criteria: Describe the class structure and key methods (fit, predict).
Explain how accuracy is computed and interpreted.
Identify the attributes stored after training (e.g., means, variances, priors).
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates provide a complete implementation perspective: the class design and the evaluation harness, which together demonstrate how to code and test Naive Bayes.

accepted.label: Sentiment Analysis: Definition and Supervised Learning
accepted.description: Sentiment analysis classifies text as positive or negative based on sentiment-bearing words. It is a supervised classification task that requires labeled data for training.
coverage_criteria: Define sentiment analysis.
Explain why labeled data is necessary for supervised sentiment analysis.
Give examples of positive and negative cue words.
accepted.merge_rationale: All four candidates introduce sentiment analysis as a text classification problem and stress the need for labeled data, forming the foundational definition of the task.

accepted.label: Bag-of-Words Representation
accepted.description: The bag-of-words model represents text as a vector of word frequencies, ignoring word order. It converts unstructured text into numerical features using a vocabulary of the most frequent words.
coverage_criteria: Explain the bag-of-words assumption (ignoring word order).
Create a BoW vector from tokenized text and a vocabulary.
Describe how to select the vocabulary size (e.g., top N words).
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates describe the bag-of-words model as a fundamental text representation technique, covering the conceptual assumption and the practical creation of feature vectors.

accepted.label: Derivation of Naive Bayes Decision Rule
accepted.description: The step-by-step derivation from Bayes theorem to the final classification formula: select class c that maximizes P(c) * ∏ P(word|c).
coverage_criteria: Write the final decision rule formula.
Explain the steps: posterior maximization, dropping the denominator, independence assumption.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering the derivation.

accepted.label: Naive Bayes Training: Prior and Likelihood Computation
accepted.description: How to compute prior class probabilities P(c) = Nc/N and word likelihoods P(word|c) as relative frequency in class c.
coverage_criteria: Calculate prior from class counts.
Calculate word likelihoods from training documents.
accepted.merge_rationale: These two calculations form the components learned during Naive Bayes training.

accepted.label: Laplace Smoothing in Naive Bayes
accepted.description: Adding a constant (usually 1) to all word counts to avoid zero probabilities for unseen words, using the formula (count + 1) / (total words + vocabulary size).
coverage_criteria: Explain the zero probability problem.
Apply Laplace smoothing to word count tables.
accepted.merge_rationale: Two candidates describe the same technique with near-identical content.

accepted.label: Logarithmic Transformation for Numerical Stability
accepted.description: Using the log of the Naive Bayes product to convert it into a sum, preventing underflow from multiplying many small probabilities.
coverage_criteria: Explain why log-sum avoids underflow.
Transform a product expression into a log-sum.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering log transformation.

accepted.label: Stop Words Removal
accepted.description: Filtering out common words (e.g., 'the', 'is') that carry little semantic value, using predefined lists such as NLTK's stopwords.
coverage_criteria: Identify common stop words.
Remove stop words from text using NLTK.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates cover the same preprocessing step with identical intent.

accepted.label: Basic Text Cleaning
accepted.description: Lowercasing text and removing HTML tags, special characters, and punctuation to reduce noise and ensure uniformity.
coverage_criteria: Explain why lowercasing and removing special characters helps text analysis.
Apply cleaning to a raw text sample.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering this initial preprocessing step.

accepted.label: Stemming
accepted.description: Reducing words to their root form (e.g., 'running' → 'run') to consolidate terms, using algorithms like SnowballStemmer from NLTK.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of stemming.
Apply a stemmer to a list of words.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering stemming.

accepted.label: Binary Multinomial Naive Bayes
accepted.description: A variant that uses binary features (word presence/absence) instead of word counts, emphasizing occurrence over frequency.
coverage_criteria: Contrast binary and frequency-based Naive Bayes.
Explain when binary features might be useful.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate describing this variant.

accepted.label: Word-level Tokenization
accepted.description: Splitting raw text into individual words (tokens) as the first step of NLP pipelines, often using functions like d2l.tokenize.
coverage_criteria: Tokenize a sentence into words.
Explain why tokenization is necessary.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering tokenization.

accepted.label: Vocabulary Construction and Out-of-Vocabulary Handling
accepted.description: Building a vocabulary from training tokens with a minimum frequency filter, and ignoring unknown words during testing to avoid errors.
coverage_criteria: Create a vocabulary with frequency filters.
Explain the strategy for handling OOV words.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates address complementary aspects of managing word sets in text classification.

accepted.label: Natural Language Processing (NLP) Definition
accepted.description: NLP is a subfield of AI focused on enabling computers to process and analyze human language, applied to tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis.
coverage_criteria: Define NLP.
Give an example of an NLP task.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate providing a foundational definition.

accepted.label: Bag of Words with CountVectorizer
accepted.description: Converting preprocessed text into a numerical matrix of token counts using scikit-learn's CountVectorizer, often with max_features to limit vocabulary size.
coverage_criteria: Transform a list of texts into a BoW matrix using CountVectorizer.
Explain the role of the max_features parameter.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate demonstrating feature extraction.

accepted.label: Fundamentos do Naive Bayes
accepted.description: Compreensão do teorema de Bayes, da suposição de independência ingênua, e como eles formam a base do classificador Naive Bayes para classificação de texto.
coverage_criteria: Enunciar o teorema de Bayes e aplicá-lo à classificação.
Explicar a suposição de independência e sua implicação na fatoração de P(X|y).
Calcular a probabilidade de classe dado um exemplo a partir de frequências de termos.
accepted.merge_rationale: Esses três candidatos cobrem aspectos complementares da base teórica do Naive Bayes: o teorema, a fatoração matemática e a visão geral do algoritmo.

accepted.label: Aplicação do Multinomial Naive Bayes em scikit-learn
accepted.description: Implementação prática do classificador MultinomialNB para análise de sentimento ou detecção de spam, incluindo preparação dos dados e treinamento.
coverage_criteria: Justificar a escolha do MultinomialNB para dados de contagem de palavras.
Carregar e pré-processar um dataset de texto para classificação.
Treinar um modelo MultinomialNB e fazer predições.
accepted.merge_rationale: Um candidato explica a adequação do algoritmo, enquanto o outro fornece um passo a passo completo de implementação; juntos formam um conceito prático coeso.

accepted.label: Divisão treino-teste para avaliação de modelos
accepted.description: Particionamento dos dados em conjuntos de treino e teste para avaliar a generalização do modelo e detectar overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Explicar a necessidade de separar os dados.
Utilizar train_test_split do scikit-learn.
Discutir o que ocorre se não houver divisão (overfitting).
accepted.merge_rationale: Ambos abordam a mesma técnica de divisão treino-teste, um com foco em acurácia e outro na validação.

accepted.label: Métricas de avaliação para classificação
accepted.description: Métricas derivadas da matriz de confusão: acurácia, precisão, recall, F1-score, para avaliar o desempenho de classificadores binários.
coverage_criteria: Definir matriz de confusão e os termos VP, FP, VN, FN.
Calcular acurácia, precisão, recall e F1-score a partir da matriz.
Interpretar o significado de cada métrica.
accepted.merge_rationale: Este candidato cobre de forma autônoma as métricas de avaliação padrão.

accepted.label: Ajuste de hiperparâmetros com GridSearchCV
accepted.description: Busca exaustiva dos melhores hiperparâmetros usando validação cruzada para otimizar o desempenho do classificador Naive Bayes.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o propósito do ajuste de hiperparâmetros.
Diferenciar Grid Search de Random Search.
Aplicar GridSearchCV no scikit-learn para encontrar os melhores parâmetros.
accepted.merge_rationale: Um único candidato aborda a técnica de tuning hyperparâmetros com exemplo prático.

accepted.label: Distribuição de classes desbalanceada
accepted.description: Identificação de conjuntos de dados com desproporção entre classes e compreensão de seu impacto na classificação.
coverage_criteria: Reconhecer um dataset desbalanceado a partir da distribuição de rótulos.
Discutir por que dados desbalanceados podem ser problemáticos.
Mencionar possíveis estratégias de mitigação.
accepted.merge_rationale: Conceito pertinente dado o exemplo prático com spam, que é naturalmente desbalanceado.
